newsitem.title: USA: U.S. retailers calm about Hong Kong handover.
newsitem.headline: U.S. retailers calm about Hong Kong handover.

text.p: Several major U.S. retailers who import Asian goods through Hong Kong said they expect little impact when the British colony reverts to Chinese rule this summer.
They said they expect the Hong Kong port to remain a major import center after the June 30 midnight handover, which will end 150 years of British rule.
J.C. Penney Co. Inc. and Federated Department Stores Inc. said they foresee no supply problems during or after the handover and plan no changes in the routes they use to import goods.
"We're not really anticipating any problems," Penney spokesman Duncan Muir said.

Like many U.S. companies, retail giants Sears and Penney receive many Chinese-made goods through Hong Kong's port. Both declined to give specific figures, but Muir said about half of the products Plano, Texas-based Penney carries are domestic and half are made outside the United States.
Federated operates more than 400 department stores including Macy's, Bon Marche, Bloomingdale's, Burdines and Lazarus. It has an office in Hong Kong to import Asian goods.
"We don't anticipate any issues at all," Federated spokeswoman Carol Sanger said.
Cincinnati-based Federated has said its strategy includes increasing emphasis on private brands.
Sears spokeswoman Jan Drummond said the Chicago-based department store chain expects a smooth Hong Kong transition.

"We do not foresee any significant commercial changes," she said. "The overriding reason for that is that between China and Hong Kong, there is a high degree of mutual need and interdependence... They are very tightly linked."

Drummond said it is estimated that about half of China's overall dollar volume of goods shipped passes through Hong Kong. She noted that China has said it plans to retain Hong Kong's currency and that many Hong Kong officials will remain in their posts.

Sears direct-imports goods both through Hong Kong and through China's Shanghai port and also buys Chinese goods from third parties, Drummond said. She said Sears has 62 employees in Hong Kong and already has 20 employees inside China.
"We feel comfortable working with the Chinese directly and so don't anticipate any significant changes," she said.

A Chicago-based manufacturer's representative for women's apparel firms, Marshall Stewart, said the companies he represents "see business as usual." He said he knew of no retailers seeking alternate supply routes.
"I don't think stores are even worried about it," he said. "Of all the stores I've talked to, no one's mentioned it."

A spokesman for a trade group of thousands of retailers, the Washington, D.C.-based National Retail Federation, agreed. "My sense is that people are not making changes," Robert Hall, the group's vice president/international trade counsel, said.
Inside and outside Hong Kong, some have expressed concern about free speech and human rights issues after the handover, and Hall said his group's members are keeping a "watchful eye" on those issues.
But, he said, members seem confident the trade and economic environment will not change dramatically.

Hong Kong Financial Secretary Donald Tsang said recently that Hong Kong will begin life as a Special Administrative Region of China in sound economic shape, "with every prospect that we will remain the most attractive business location in this region."
